extracted.intended_audience: general public and readers interested in British politics, media controversies, and public broadcasting policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and contested criteria around whether and how the BBC should invite political parties — including far-right groups — to appear on Question Time; covers editorial, legal, security, and format considerations illustrated by the Nick Griffin / BNP 2009 case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of electoral support as basis for invitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC studies the support gained in elections by each of the parties, large and small, before deciding who to invite and how frequently they should appear. Mark Thompson: 'It is a straightforward matter of fact that, with some 6% of the vote and the election of two MEPs ... the BNP has demonstrated a level of support that would normally lead to an occasional invitation to join the panel on Question Time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral performance (vote share, number of elected representatives) is used as a factual benchmark to decide occasional invitations. Frequency of invitations is tied to demonstrated support (see also later statement limiting appearances to 'probably no more than once a year').

rubrics_metrics.name: BBC charter / impartiality obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC must treat parties with impartiality and in line with its charter: Ric Bailey said the BBC 'would have been breaking its charter if it had not treated the BNP with impartiality ... We absolutely stand by that judgement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions to include parties on programmes must be defensible under the BBC's charter and impartiality requirements, not made on a desire for controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial judgement reserved to Director-General
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC Trust concluded that 'the decision as to whether it is appropriate in all the circumstances for the BBC to allow the BNP to participate on Question Time is a question of editorial judgement, which the charter and framework agreement reserve for the Director-General.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Trust frames inclusion/exclusion choices as editorial matters for senior BBC management rather than external bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with general law and editorial/regulatory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trust wrote to the Director-General asking him to 'ensure that the broadcast programme complies with the general law, the BBC's editorial guidelines and all other regulatory requirements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invitations and broadcasts must be vetted for legal compliance (e.g., hate speech laws) and adherence to internal editorial rules and external broadcast regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-recorded format mitigates some concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trust noted that 'given the pre-recorded nature of the show, many of the concerns were hypothetical and premature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-recording can reduce certain risks (e.g., live uncontrollable statements, immediate disruption) and may factor into the decision whether to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free speech / anti-censorship principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that keeping a figure off air is a parliamentary, not a BBC, matter: Mark Thompson wrote 'Keeping Nick Griffin off air is a job for parliament, not the BBC' and John Humphrys said 'Free speech is the issue here, and the BBC's obligations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One evaluative principle is that the broadcaster should avoid censorship and allow controversial voices to be heard and challenged on air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested higher entry threshold (election to national parliament)
rubrics_metrics.description: The anti-fascist magazine Searchlight argued that 'entry level for inclusion on BBC programmes should be "election to the national parliament".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commentators recommend a stricter criterion for inclusion (national parliamentary representation) to avoid giving fringe/extremist parties high-profile platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and public-safety considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about safety influenced location and security: extra Metropolitan Police officers were drafted in, 60 extra security guards were recruited, Television Centre was locked down; councils asked for clarification of security arrangements; policing cost reported as £143,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about venue, timing, and presence of controversial figures should account for public-order risks, policing requirements, and potential costs; location choice can be changed for security reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition to ensure robust scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstream party figures (e.g., Jack Straw, Baroness Warsi, Chris Huhne) participated so Griffin could be challenged; The Times noted strategy to ensure Griffin could not be given an 'easy ride.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including experienced, directly opposing panellists is a deliberate editorial tool to subject controversial guests to scrutiny rather than provide a platform without challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-set agenda and pre-selected audience questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Question Time's format: 'Questions from a local audience are directed to a panel... set-piece questions from pre-selected audience members' and 'the panellists have no previous knowledge of the content of the questions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programme topics are generated by pre-selected audience members, which affects how much producers control the agenda and can influence whether the broadcast focuses on a guest or broader topical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding programme becoming dominated by one guest ('Nick Griffin show')
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints that the programme had 'overly focused on the BNP, becoming the "Nick Griffin show".'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should seek topical balance so a single guest or issue does not dominate and allow claims of victimisation or unfair focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency limits tied to continued electoral support
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark Thompson later stated future BNP appearances on Question Time would 'probably be no more than once a year and could be less', based on the party continuing the same levels of support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when invited, frequency of appearances is constrained and should be periodically reviewed according to electoral performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding normalisation of extremist parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guardian editorial: 'The BNP is no normal party — yet by inviting it on to Question Time, the BBC runs the risk of normalising it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key evaluative concern is whether giving airtime confers legitimacy or normalisation to groups with extremist ideologies; this weighs against invitation in some views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defeating the far right through reasoned, sophisticated argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Ted Cantle urged 'a "more sophisticated approach" using reasoned arguments, to defeat the far right.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One normative criterion for broadcasting is that exposure should be paired with substantive, reasoned rebuttal rather than purely adversarial spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political parties' 'No Platform' policies vs case-by-case engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour's policy 'never to share a platform with the BNP' was changed after the BBC invitation to a 'case by case' basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Party-level policies about sharing platforms influence who attends; parties may adapt policies when public-broadcast contexts change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location and audience composition affect fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: BNP and others argued London was 'too multicultural' to be fair to the BNP; choice of location (e.g., London vs north-west) was contested as affecting the reception and fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should consider geographic and demographic composition of audience when deciding venue, as it can materially affect the balance and perceived fairness of the encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and routine production practices (audience crib-sheets)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Daily Mail alleged the BBC 'stage-managed' the programme, highlighting a crib-sheet handed out to audience members; The Guardian's 'Media Monkey' blog observed such a sheet is routinely given to the audience and accused The Mail of using a 'doctored' crib-sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine production materials (briefing sheets) can be mischaracterised as manipulation; transparency about production routines can reduce accusations of stage-managing.
